content: Preface: Why Native llama.cpp is PainfulRunning Large Language Models (LLMs) locally using llama.cpp offers incredible privacy and performance. However, deploying it effectively is notoriously difficult. The native experience is raw: compiling binaries manually, dealing with unoptimized package manager downloads, juggling 50GB file transfers, calculating mental VRAM boundaries, and memorizing arcane CLI flags. Get a single context metric wrong, and your GPU violently crashes with an Out-Of-Memory (OOM) panic. We built an all-in-one Go application—llama_manager.go—to solve this entirely. It is a highly fault-tolerant daemon that dynamically profiles physical hardware, reverse-engineers a model’s memory footprint on the fly, and calculates the exact parameters needed to run engines at absolute peak efficiency. Here is the architectural Masterclass on the 1000+ lines of Go logic driving the system.
title: The Golang4U LLM Bible: Internals of the Intelligent Llama Manager

content: 3.2 The Stream Hijacker (Live Progress Bar)A custom io.Writer interface violently hijacks the data stream output to provide live feedback by rewriting the active console line via carriage returns (\r\033[K) without gobbling RAM allocations. type progressWriter struct { io.Writer TotalDownloaded int64 TotalSize int64 LastPercent int64 } func (pw *progressWriter) Write(p []byte) (int, error) { n, err := pw.Writer.Write(p) pw.TotalDownloaded += int64(n) if pw.TotalSize > 0 { percent := (pw.TotalDownloaded * 100) / pw.TotalSize if percent > pw.LastPercent { fmt.Printf("\r\033[KDownloading... %d%% (%d MB / %d MB) - Press Ctrl+C to Pause", percent, pw.TotalDownloaded/(1024*1024), pw.TotalSize/(1024*1024)) pw.LastPercent = percent } } return n, err }

content: 3.3 HTTP 206 Resumable Block ChunkingIf an interruption occurs, we write the data to a .part chunk. Upon restarting the request, we modify the TCP/IP Headers (HTTP Range) to bypass the previously collected bits and stream directly into os.O_APPEND. func downloadWithResume(ctx context.Context, dlURL, finalDest string) error { partDest := finalDest + ".part" var startBytes int64 = 0 if info, err := os.Stat(partDest); err == nil { startBytes = info.Size() // Existing chunk! } req, _ := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, "GET", dlURL, nil) if startBytes > 0 { req.Header.Set("Range", fmt.Sprintf("bytes=%d-", startBytes)) // Resume! } resp, _ := dlClient.Do(req) flags := os.O_CREATE | os.O_WRONLY if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusPartialContent { flags |= os.O_APPEND // Append if Supported } else { flags |= os.O_TRUNC // Truncate and Restart } outFile, _ := os.OpenFile(partDest, flags, 0644) // ... Copy stream via pw }

content: 5.1 KV Cache Formating & Sub-Slot Slicing KV Cache Quantization (-ctk, -ctv): We format memory blocks optionally using 4-Bit arrays (q4_0), squeezing cache volumes down by over 75% for massive prompt windowing. Anti-Hyperthreading Optimization (-t): By halving CPU core threads mathematically (Total Cores / 2), we force llama.cpp to bind exclusively to distinct physical logic gates, bypassing hyper-threaded cache thrashing entirely. Context Slicing Prevention (-np 1): Default daemon topologies eagerly aggressively chop memory context slots for multiple parallel tenant users. We enforce single tenant (-kvu) locks. Batching & Defragmentation: llama.cpp evaluates tokens optimally at 512 chunks. The user can ramp batch (-b, -ub) sizing up to 2048 to significantly reduce Initial Time-to-First-Token processing. We inject --defrag-thold 0.1 to heal degraded memory fragmentation pools automatically.

We heal the app state dynamically: func isProcessAlive(pid int) bool { if runtime.GOOS == "windows" { cmd := exec.Command("tasklist", "/FI", fmt.Sprintf("PID eq %d", pid)) out, _ := cmd.Output() return strings.Contains(string(out), strconv.Itoa(pid)) } process, err := os.FindProcess(pid) if err != nil { return false } return process.Signal(syscall.Signal(0)) == nil // Ping kernel payload zero check }

content: 5.4 Graceful Zero-Leak VRAM Signal ChannelsIf a user violently slams Ctrl+C into the foreground terminal, the Go layer will inherently drop execution silently. However, C++ binaries hold GPU architectures captive. A dropped pointer implies absolute VRAM lock, requiring PC reboots. content: Your code is correct, but your server is vulnerable. We explore the critical runtime tunings: GOMEMLIMIT, Slowloris Timeouts, and Database Connection Pooling to prevent OOM kills and DDoS attacks.
title: The Golang4U Hardening Bible: DDoS-Proofing & OOM Prevention

content: Preface: The “Correct” Code that CrashesYou can write perfect algorithms, but if you deploy them with default settings, you will crash. Default HTTP Server: Vulnerable to Slowloris. Default GC: Vulnerable to OOM Killers. Default DB Driver: Vulnerable to Connection Storms. This guide is about Runtime Hardening.
title: The Golang4U Hardening Bible: DDoS-Proofing & OOM Prevention

content: Chapter 1: The Slowloris Attack (Timeouts)The Attack: A hacker opens 1,000 connections to your server. They send: G… wait 10s … E … wait 10s … T … The default Go http.Server has NO Timeout. It will wait forever. Your RAM fills up with open connections. The server hangs. The Fix: Explicit Timeouts in internal/server/server.go. func (s *Server) BeginServer() { srv := &http.Server{ Addr: ":8080", Handler: s.e, // Echo instance // 1. ReadTimeout: How long to wait for the Request Body ReadTimeout: 5 * time.Second, // 2. WriteTimeout: How long to write the Response WriteTimeout: 10 * time.Second, // 3. IdleTimeout: How long to keep Keep-Alive connections open IdleTimeout: 120 * time.Second, } // 4. HeaderTimeout (Go 1.18+): Prevent Slowloris on Headers srv.ReadHeaderTimeout = 2 * time.Second srv.ListenAndServe() } Now, if a hacker pauses for more than 2 seconds while typing GET /, we cut the connection. Golang4U is now Slowloris-proof.
title: The Golang4U Hardening Bible: DDoS-Proofing & OOM Prevention

content: Chapter 2: The memory Killer (OOM)Go is a Garbage Collected language. By default, the GC triggers when the heap doubles in size (GOGC=100). The Scenario: Your container has 1GB RAM. Your app uses 600MB. A request comes in. Heap grows to 700MB. GC Target is $600MB \times 2 = 1.2GB$. The App tries to allocate up to 1.2GB. Linux OOM Killer sees usage > 1GB. KILL -9. App crashes. The Fix: GOMEMLIMIT (Go 1.19+). We tell the Go runtime exactly how much RAM it has. In cmd/server/main.go (or Docker env): export GOMEMLIMIT=450MiB Now, if usage hits 450MB, the GC becomes aggressive. It runs continuously to stay under 450MB. It sacrifices CPU to save RAM. The App slows down, but it does NOT crash.
title: The Golang4U Hardening Bible: DDoS-Proofing & OOM Prevention

content: Chapter 3: The Connection Storm (DB Pooling)By default, the Mongo driver might open 100+ connections if load spikes. If you have 10 instances of your app, that’s 1,000 connections to Mongo. Mongo crashes. The Fix: Explicit Pooling in internal/database/mongo_database.go (Configurable). func NewMongoDatabase(..., maxPoolSize uint64, maxConnIdleTime string) { opts := options.Client().ApplyURI(uri) // 1. MaxPoolSize: Hard limit on active connections opts.SetMaxPoolSize(maxPoolSize) // 2. MaxConnIdleTime: Close unused connections dur, _ := time.ParseDuration(maxConnIdleTime) opts.SetMaxConnIdleTime(dur) client, _ := mongo.Connect(opts) } Configuration (config.yaml or ENV): db_max_pool_size: 50 db_max_conn_idle_time: "5m" This acts as a “Circuit Breaker”. It adapts to your infrastructure size.
title: The Golang4U Hardening Bible: DDoS-Proofing & OOM Prevention

content: Chapter 4: Docker Resource LimitsFinally, we enforce these limits at the Kernel level. docker-compose.yml: services: app: # 1. CPU Quota: Prevents one container from eating the whole server cpus: "1.0" # 2. Hard Memory Limit: The wall (OOM Killer triggers here) mem_limit: 1024m # 3. Soft Memory Limit: Warns the OS mem_reservation: 512m environment: - GOMEMLIMIT=900MiB # 90% of Hard Limit Why 90%? Go runtime needs RAM. But the OS also needs RAM (stacks, pointers, file descriptors). Allow 10-15% headroom for “Non-Heap” memory.
title: The Golang4U Hardening Bible: DDoS-Proofing & OOM Prevention

content: ConclusionA Production-Ready service is: Impatient: It drops slow connections (ReadTimeout). Self-Aware: It knows its memory limits (GOMEMLIMIT). Polite: It doesn’t overwhelm the DB (MaxPoolSize). These “Expert Control Measures” are the difference between a 3AM page and a good night’s sleep.
title: The Golang4U Hardening Bible: DDoS-Proofing & OOM Prevention

content: How to organize business logic. We explore the 'Rich Model' pattern in Golang4U, contrasting the `User` domain entity with the `Store` persistence wrapper, and deep dive into the Referral Code generation algorithms.
title: The Golang4U Domain Bible: Structs, Validation & Rich Models

content: Preface: Where does logic belong?In architecture, there is a concept called “Anemic Domain Model”. This is when your structs are just data bags: type User struct { Name string } And all your logic is in Service: func (s *Service) IsAdult(u *User) bool { return u.Age >= 18 } Golang4U prefers a Rich Domain Model. We put logic on the struct itself when it applies to the entity. func (u *User) IsAdult() bool { return u.Age >= 18 } This guide explores libs/user/user.go.
title: The Golang4U Domain Bible: Structs, Validation & Rich Models

content: Chapter 1: The Great Store/User SplitWe do not map our Database Document 1:1 to our User representation. This is a critical separation.
title: The Golang4U Domain Bible: Structs, Validation & Rich Models

content: 1.1 The User (The Person)This struct represents the “Business Entity”. It has a Profile, Initials, Bio. It is what we think of when we say “User”. type User struct { Profile Profile `json:"profile"` Country string `json:"country"` // ... }
title: The Golang4U Domain Bible: Structs, Validation & Rich Models

content: 1.2 The Store (The Record)This struct represents “How we save it”. It wraps the User with System Metadata. type Store struct { User User `bson:"user"` // Embedded Domain Entity Disable bool `bson:"disable"` // System Flag (Banned?) Lifetime time.Time `bson:"lifetime"` // TTL (Delete after 1 hour?) ReferalCodes []ReferalCode `bson:"referal_codes"` // Private Data } Why? The User struct is often sent to the Frontend (serialized to JSON). The Store struct is NEVER sent to the Frontend. This prevents us from accidentally leaking ReferalCodes or Disable status in an API response. The types themselves enforce security.
title: The Golang4U Domain Bible: Structs, Validation & Rich Models

content: Chapter 2: The Referral AlgorithmGolang4U has a Invite-Only system. This is complex domain logic. It lives in libs/user/user.go.
title: The Golang4U Domain Bible: Structs, Validation & Rich Models

content: 2.1 Generating Codes (Collision Avoidance) func (*Store) CreateReferalCodes(user *User, numOfCodes int) []ReferalCode { codes := []ReferalCode{} for i := 0; i < numOfCodes; i++ { // Generating a unique hash based on User + Counter + Random temp := randomHasherForCodes(user, i)[0:8] // Internal Collision Check // (Ensure we didn't generate the same code twice in this batch) for j := 0; j < len(codes)-1; j++ { if collision { regenerate() } } codes = append(codes, ReferalCode{ Code: user.AvatarName + "-" + temp, Lifetime: time.Now().Unix(), }) } return codes } This logic belongs on the Store struct because it manipulates the internal state of the Record. It doesn’t need a Database connection or an HTTP request; it is pure logic.
title: The Golang4U Domain Bible: Structs, Validation & Rich Models

content: 2.2 Reclaiming SpaceWe also have logic to remove codes: func (*User) RemoveReferal(s []ReferalCode, r string) []ReferalCode { // Slice manipulation logic // ... return append(s[:i], s[i+1:]...) } By keeping this slice math in libs/user, the Service layer remains clean. Service: “User, remove code X.” User: “Done.”
title: The Golang4U Domain Bible: Structs, Validation & Rich Models

content: Chapter 3: Struct Tags (The Rosetta Stone)Go structs often have to talk to multiple languages (JSON, BSON, YAML, Validation). We use Struct Tags to define these translations. AvatarName string `yaml:"avatar_name" json:"avatar_name" validate:"required,alphanum" bson:"avatar_name"` json: For the Frontend API. bson: For MongoDB. yaml: For Config files (in some cases). validate: For the Validator library. The Power of Centralization: We define validation rules (“Required, Alphanumeric”) right next to the field data. We don’t write if len(name) == 0 checks in handlers. The request binds to the struct, the validator reads the tag, and it auto-rejects invalid data.
title: The Golang4U Domain Bible: Structs, Validation & Rich Models

content: ConclusionA codebase is manageable only when logic lives where it belongs. Persistence Logic: In Store. Entity Logic: In User. Orchestration Logic: In Service. By treating libs/user as a “Rich Model”, Golang4U keeps its Services thin and its Data structures smart.
title: The Golang4U Domain Bible: Structs, Validation & Rich Models

content: How to build a reliable email system using only the Go standard library. We explore `net/smtp`, HTML template composition, and the architecture of our Magic Link and Verification systems.

content: Preface: The Vendor TrapEvery startup guide tells you: “Sign up for SendGrid/Mailgun/AWS SES.” Result involved? Complexity: You need to manage API keys, webhooks, and SDKs. Cost: They get expensive fast. Lock-in: Switching from SendGrid to Mailgun requires rewriting code. In Golang4U, we choose the Standard Library. Go’s net/smtp is battle-hardened. It speaks the raw protocol of the internet. This guide shows how we built a Vendor-Agnostic emailer.
title: The Golang4U Email Bible: Native SMTP & Transactional Systems

content: Chapter 1: The SMTP Protocol (Raw & Real)Sending an email is just a TCP handshake. Connect to Port 587 (Submission). EHLO golang4u.com. STARTTLS (Upgrade to Encryption). AUTH PLAIN .... MAIL FROM: .... RCPT TO: .... DATA.
title: The Golang4U Email Bible: Native SMTP & Transactional Systems

content: 1.1 The Code (internal/emailer/email.go)We wrap this complexity in a simple function: func SendEmail(addr, from, password string, to []string, msg []byte) error { // 1. Setup Auth auth := smtp.PlainAuth("", from, password, "smtp.gmail.com") // 2. Send (Handles Handshake, TLS, Auth, Data) return smtp.SendMail(addr, auth, from, to, msg) } Why Gmail? For our current scale, Gmail’s SMTP is reliable and free. Because we interact with the Standard SMTP Protocol, swapping Gmail for AWS SES SMTP Endpoint is a 1-line config change (just change the addr). No code rewrite needed.

2.1 The Magic Link Template (user_service.u)We use Magic Links for passwordless login. The email body must be: Secure: The link contains a high-entropy token. Clear: A big green button. Responsive: Works on Mobile. func SendMagicLinkEmail(...) { body := fmt.Sprintf(`

Login to Golang4u

Click below. Valid for 15 minutes.

Log In Now `, link) } Why fmt.Sprintf? For simple transactional emails, a full template engine (html/template) can be overkill. fmt.Sprintf is faster and, since the input (link) is generated by us (Hex Token), there is no XSS risk. Note: If injecting User Name, ALWAYS use html/template to prevent injection.
title: The Golang4U Email Bible: Native SMTP & Transactional Systems

content: Chapter 3: Verification Logic (The “On-Time” Link)When a user registers, we send a “Verify Account” email. This is implemented in SendOnTimeLinkEmail.
title: The Golang4U Email Bible: Native SMTP & Transactional Systems

content: 3.1 The “Disposable Email” CheckBefore we even send, we check if the email is garbage. VerifyEmail in email.go: func VerifyEmail(emailAddr string) error { parts := strings.Split(emailAddr, "@") if len(parts) != 2 { return Error("Invalid Format") } // Future Expansion: Check MX Records // _, err := net.LookupMX(parts[1]) } This saves our reputation score. Sending emails to non-existent domains hurts deliverability.
title: The Golang4U Email Bible: Native SMTP & Transactional Systems

content: Chapter 4: Handling SecretsWe need a password to talk to the SMTP server. NEVER hardcode this. In internal/handler/handler.go: h.GmailToken = config.GmailToken This flows from: OS Env Var (GMAIL_TOKEN) -> config.Load() -> Handler -> SendEmail. This ensures that our source code is safe to open-source, even if our production credentials are secret.
title: The Golang4U Email Bible: Native SMTP & Transactional Systems

content: ConclusionYou don’t need a SaaS subscription to send emails. The internet was built on open protocols like SMTP. By using net/smtp, Golang4U achieves: Zero Cost: Free tier SMTP. Zero Dependency: No 3rd party Go SDKs. Maximum Portability: Switch providers in seconds. This is the definition of “Cloud Native” — portable and resilient.
title: The Golang4U Email Bible: Native SMTP & Transactional Systems

content: How to handle file uploads without getting hacked. We explore Magic Byte detection, Streaming Virus Scanning (ClamAV), and how to block malware at the network edge before it hits your disk.
title: The Golang4U File Upload Bible: Streaming to ClamAV

content: Preface: The Upload VulnerabilityAccepting user content is necessary but dangerous. A “Profile Picture” upload form is often a backdoor for: Shell Uploads: Uploading shell.php to execute code. Malware Distribution: Hosting a standard Windows virus on your domain. DoS Attacks: Uploading a 50GB file to fill your disk. In Golang4U, we treat every file as a potential bomb. This guide explains how we defuse them using Streaming and ClamAV.
title: The Golang4U File Upload Bible: Streaming to ClamAV

content: Chapter 1: The Magic Bytes (Trust Nothing)First rule: Never trust the file extension. A file named cute_cat.jpg might actually be a .exe. A file named report.pdf might be a shell script.
title: The Golang4U File Upload Bible: Streaming to ClamAV

content: 1.1 Content-Type SniffingBrowser headers (Content-Type: image/jpeg) are sent by the user. They are easily faked. We must look at the first 512 bytes of the file (The Header). In internal/handler/handler.go: func isImageFile(b []byte) bool { // 1. Read the first 512 bytes // (http.DetectContentType needs at most 512) if len(b) < 512 { return false // Too small to be a valid image } // 2. Sniff contentType := http.DetectContentType(b[:512]) // 3. Validation return strings.HasPrefix(contentType, "image/") } This function looks for “Magic Bytes” (Signatures). JPEG: FF D8 FF PNG: 89 50 4E 47 GIF: 47 49 46 38 If a user uploads malware.exe renamed to image.png, DetectContentType will see the MZ header of the executable and return application/octet-stream. We reject it.
title: The Golang4U File Upload Bible: Streaming to ClamAV

content: Chapter 2: The ClamAV IntegrationChecking extensions is not enough. A valid PDF can contain a malicious script. A valid JPEG can contain an exploit. We need an Antivirus. We use ClamAV, the open-source industry standard.
title: The Golang4U File Upload Bible: Streaming to ClamAV

content: 2.1 The ArchitectureWe do not run ClamAV inside our Go binary. That would be slow. We run clamd as a separate microservice (Docker container). Our Go app talks to it over TCP.
title: The Golang4U File Upload Bible: Streaming to ClamAV

content: 2.2 Streaming vs BufferingThe naive way: User uploads 10MB file. Server saves to /tmp/upload.jpg. Server calls clamscan /tmp/upload.jpg. Server deletes if bad. Problem: You just saved malware to your disk. What if the clamscan process crashes? The malware sits there. The Golang4U Streaming Way: User starts upload. Server opens a Pipe to ClamAV. As bytes arrive from User, we copy them directly to ClamAV. We never save the full file until ClamAV says “OK”.
title: The Golang4U File Upload Bible: Streaming to ClamAV

content: 2.3 The Code (internal/fileScan/filescan.go) func (fs *FileScan) ScanData(c echo.Context, b []byte) error { // 1. Connect to ClamAV cld := clamd.NewClamd(fs.clamdUrl) if err := cld.Ping(); err != nil { // Fail Secure: If AV is down, no uploads allowed. return Error("AV Service Unavailable") } // 2. The Multi-Reader Trick // We need to read the body TWICE. // Once for ClamAV, and (if clean) once for the actual Application. // So we read it into a buffer. bodyBytes, _ := io.ReadAll(c.Request().Body) // Restore the body for the next handler c.Request().Body = io.NopCloser(bytes.NewBuffer(bodyBytes)) // 3. Stream to ClamAV // We create a Reader from our bytes and pipe it to ClamAV response, err := cld.ScanStream(bytes.NewReader(bodyBytes), make(chan bool)) // 4. Process Result for res := range response { if res.Status == "FOUND" { // MALWARE DETECTED! return fs.BlockUser(c) } } return nil // Clean }
title: The Golang4U File Upload Bible: Streaming to ClamAV

content: Chapter 3: Automated Response (The IP Ban)If someone uploads a virus, it wasn’t an accident. It was an attack. We don’t just say “Upload Failed.” We strike back. func (fs *FileScan) BlockUser(c echo.Context) error { ip := c.RealIP() fmt.Printf("Malware detected from IP: %s. BANNING.\n", ip) // Call our Locking IPFilter fs.ipBlockList.BlockIP(ip) return c.String(403, "Malware Detected. You have been banned.") } This effectively turns our File Upload endpoint into a Honeypot. Attacker tries a test upload. We detect it. We ban their IP instantly. They cannot try a second payload.
title: The Golang4U File Upload Bible: Streaming to ClamAV

content: Chapter 4: Defense in Depth (Docker Limit)What if they try to upload a 50GB file to exhaust our RAM? ClamAV streaming handles memory well, but io.ReadAll puts it in RAM. We configure Echo to limit body size. // internal/server/server.go e.Use(middleware.BodyLimit("10M")) And in Docker-Compose: services: app: mem_limit: 512m If a request exceeds 10MB, the connection is severed before it hits our handler.
title: The Golang4U File Upload Bible: Streaming to ClamAV

content: ConclusionSecure file handling is about Distrust. Distrust Headers: We check Magic Bytes. Distrust Content: We stream to ClamAV. Distrust Intent: We auto-ban users who fail the scan. This “Paranoid Architecture” keeps the server clean.
title: The Golang4U File Upload Bible: Streaming to ClamAV

content: A deep dive into implementing Two-Factor Authentication. We analyze the 3-phase Setup-Activate-Persist cycle, the use of Time-Based One-Time Passwords (TOTP), and the caching strategies used to prevent lockout states.
title: The Golang4U 2FA Bible: TOTP, QR Codes & State Machines

content: Preface: The 3 Factors of AuthAuthentication is proving you are who you say you are. There are 3 ways to do this: Something you Know (Knowledge): Password, PIN, Mother’s Maiden Name. Something you Have (Possession): Phone, YubiKey, RSA Token. Something you Are (Inherence): Fingerprint, FaceID, Retina. A Password alone is weak because it can be phished. 2FA (Two-Factor) combines #1 and #2. Even if a hacker phishes your password, they cannot physically steal your phone over the internet.
title: The Golang4U 2FA Bible: TOTP, QR Codes & State Machines

content: Chapter 1: The TOTP Standard (RFC 6238)We use TOTP (Time-based One-Time Password). This is the standard used by Google Authenticator, Authy, etc.
title: The Golang4U 2FA Bible: TOTP, QR Codes & State Machines

content: 1.1 The MathIt is a function of Time ($T$) and a Secret Keys ($K$). $$OTP = Truncate(HMAC_{SHA1}(K, \lfloor \frac{CurrentTime}{30} \rfloor))$$ Step 1: Get Unix Epoch Time (seconds since 1970). Step 2: Divide by 30 (floor). This creates a “Time Step”. The code is valid for 30 seconds. Step 3: Hash the Step with the Secret Key ($K$). Step 4: Take the last 4 bits of the hash to find an offset. Step 5: Extract 4 bytes from the hash at that offset. Step 6: Modulo 1,000,000 to get a 6-digit number.
title: The Golang4U 2FA Bible: TOTP, QR Codes & State Machines

content: 1.2 The “Shared Secret”The magic is that both the Server and your Phone perform this same math independently. They only need to share $K$ once (via the QR Code).
title: The Golang4U 2FA Bible: TOTP, QR Codes & State Machines

content: Chapter 2: The Implementation (internal/service)The biggest risk in 2FA is User Lockout. If we enable 2FA on the account before the user has successfully scanned the QR code, and their camera breaks… they are locked out forever. We implement a 3-Phase Commit Protocol.
title: The Golang4U 2FA Bible: TOTP, QR Codes & State Machines

content: Phase 1: Setup (The Proposal)User visits /2fa/setup. We generate the secret, but we DO NOT save it to the user profile yet. // internal/service/user_service.go func (s *UserService) Setup2FA(username string) ([]byte, error) { // 1. Generate Random Secret (20 bytes) otp, _ := twofactor.NewTOTP(username, "Golang4U", crypto.SHA1, 6) // 2. Serialize Secret secretBytes, _ := otp.ToBytes() // This is "K" // 3. Store in TTL Cache (Temporary!) // We store it for 10 minutes. If they don't finish setup, it vanishes. s.ttlDB.Set(username+"_2fa_pending", secretBytes, 10*time.Minute) // 4. Return QR Code (PNG) return otp.QR() }
title: The Golang4U 2FA Bible: TOTP, QR Codes & State Machines

content: Phase 2: Activation (The Proof)User scans QR, types 123456. Sends to /2fa/activate. func (s *UserService) Activate2FA(username, pin string) error { // 1. Retrieve Pending Secret from Cache item := s.ttlDB.Get(username + "_2fa_pending") if item == nil { return Error("Setup Expired. Start over.") } // 2. Validate The PIN // Does math(Secret, Time) == pin? secret := item.Value().([]byte) valid := twofactor.Validate(secret, pin) if !valid { return Error("Wrong Code") } // 3. COMMIT (Persistence) // NOW we save it to the DB. user.Profile.TwoFactorSecret = secret s.repo.Save(user) // 4. Cleanup s.ttlDB.Delete(username + "_2fa_pending") return nil } This guarantees that 2FA is only enabled if the user has proved they can generate codes.
title: The Golang4U 2FA Bible: TOTP, QR Codes & State Machines

content: Phase 3: Verification (The Login)In internal/handler/login.go: func (h *Handler) Login(...) { // Check Password... OK. if len(user.TwoFactorSecret) > 0 { // 2FA is Enabled. // DO NOT return Access Token. // Return a "Temporary Auth Token". return c.JSON(200, { "status": "2fa_required", "temp_token": "..." // Only valid for /verify-2fa endpoint }) } }
title: The Golang4U 2FA Bible: TOTP, QR Codes & State Machines

content: Chapter 3: Time Drift & WindowingClocks are not perfect. The user’s phone might be 5 seconds fast. The server might be 2 seconds slow. If we only check the exact 30-second window, valid codes might fail at the boundary (e.g., at 12:00:29 vs 12:00:30). The Solution: Windowing. We verify the Current Window ($T$), the Previous Window ($T-1$), and the Next Window ($T+1$). This gives a $\pm 30$ second tolerance. // twofactor library does this automatically otp.Validate(pin) // Checks T, T-1, T+1
title: The Golang4U 2FA Bible: TOTP, QR Codes & State Machines

content: Chapter 4: Recovery (The “Bus Factor”)Phones break. Users lose them. A robust system MUST provide Recovery Codes. Generation: When 2FA is activated, we generate 10 random strings: A1B2-C3D4. Storage: We Hash them (bcrypt). We treat them like 10 one-time passwords. Usage: User enters code. We check hashes. Match? Log them in AND Delete that code. This ensures that even if someone sees your printed recovery sheet, they can only use each code once (though they shouldn’t see it at all!).
title: The Golang4U 2FA Bible: TOTP, QR Codes & State Machines

content: ConclusionImplementing 2FA is a responsibility. It adds friction to the user experience in exchange for massive security gains. Our implementation focuses on Availability: TTL Cache prevents “Ghost” setups. Windowing prevents “My code was right!” frustration. Recovery codes prevents “I lost my phone” support tickets. This completes the Auth lifecycle for Golang4U.
title: The Golang4U 2FA Bible: TOTP, QR Codes & State Machines

content: Going beyond HTTPS. A technical deep dive into how `golang4u` implements application-layer encryption using ECIES (Elliptic Curve Integrated Encryption Scheme) to protect sensitive user payload from the browser to the database.
title: The Golang4U Cryptography Bible: E2EE, ECIES & Blind Indexing

content: Preface: Why TLS is Not EnoughHTTPS (TLS 1.3) protects data “In Transit.” It prevents the Hacker in the Coffee Shop from reading your password. But it does not protect against: Malicious Proxies: A corporate proxy (MITM) that terminates TLS. The Server Itself: If our logs accidentally print req.Body. Memory Dumps: If the server crashes and dumps RAM. To fix this, we implement End-to-End Encryption (E2EE) at the Application Layer. The password is encrypted in the browser and only decrypted inside the Service function.
title: The Golang4U Cryptography Bible: E2EE, ECIES & Blind Indexing

content: Chapter 1: The Cryptographic SuiteWe chose standard, NIST-approved algorithms to ensure broad compatibility (especially with browser WebCrypto API).
title: The Golang4U Cryptography Bible: E2EE, ECIES & Blind Indexing

content: 1.1 Asymmetric: ECDH (P-256) Algorithm: Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman. Curve: NIST P-256 (also known as prime256v1). Why?: Native hardware acceleration on x86/ARM. Built-in to Chrome/Firefox/Safari.
title: The Golang4U Cryptography Bible: E2EE, ECIES & Blind Indexing

content: 1.2 Symmetric: AES-GCM (256-bit) Algorithm: Advanced Encryption Standard. Mode: Galois/Counter Mode (GCM). Why?: Authenticated Encryption (AEAD). It protects both Secrecy (Reading) and Integrity (Tampering). If you flip a bit in the ciphertext, decryption fails; it doesn’t just produce garbage.
title: The Golang4U Cryptography Bible: E2EE, ECIES & Blind Indexing

content: Chapter 2: ECIES (Elliptic Curve Integrated Encryption Scheme)Public Key crypto (ECC) is slow. You can’t encrypt a 1MB file with it. Symmetric crypto (AES) is fast. But you can’t share the key safely. ECIES is the “Hybrid” answer.
title: The Golang4U Cryptography Bible: E2EE, ECIES & Blind Indexing

content: 2.1 The Handshake (The Math)Let’s assume Alice (Browser) sends data to Bob (Server). Bob has a static keypair: $(b, B)$ where $B = b \times G$. Alice generates ephemeral keypair: $(a, A)$ where $A = a \times G$. Alice computes Shared Secret $S$: $$S = a \times B = a \times (b \times G)$$ Bob computes Shared Secret $S$: $$S = b \times A = b \times (a \times G)$$ $$(ab)G = (ba)G$$ They now share the secret $S$ (the coordinate on the curve) without ever transmitting it. 5. Alice derives key $K = KDF(S)$. 6. Alice encrypts message $C = AES_{GCM}(M, K)$. 7. Alice sends: $[A] + [Nonce] + [C]$.
title: The Golang4U Cryptography Bible: E2EE, ECIES & Blind Indexing

content: Chapter 3: The Implementation (internal/security)
title: The Golang4U Cryptography Bible: E2EE, ECIES & Blind Indexing

content: 3.1 Backend Key Loading (LoadOrGenerateKey)We need a persistent identity. In internal/security/keys.go: func LoadOrGenerateKey(path string) (*ecdh.PrivateKey, error) { // 1. Try Read PEM from Disk // ... // 2. Generate New (P-256) priv, err := ecdh.P256().GenerateKey(rand.Reader) // 3. Save to Disk (PEM encoded) // ... return priv, nil } This Key is the “Server Identity”.
title: The Golang4U Cryptography Bible: E2EE, ECIES & Blind Indexing

content: 3.2 The Decryption Function (DecryptECIES)When the server receives the payload, it must unpack it. Our format is critical: Uncompressed_Pub_Key (65 bytes) || Nonce (12 bytes) || Ciphertext. func DecryptECIES(serverPriv *ecdh.PrivateKey, payloadHex string) ([]byte, error) { // 1. Decode Hex data, _ := hex.DecodeString(payloadHex) // 2. Extract Parts clientPubBytes := data[:65] nonce := data[65:77] ciphertext := data[77:] // 3. Parse Client Ephemeral Public Key clientPub, _ := ecdh.P256().NewPublicKey(clientPubBytes) // 4. ECDH (Perform the math) sharedSecret, _ := serverPriv.ECDH(clientPub) // 5. Decrypt using Shared Secret as AES Key // (Note: In production we use HKDF on sharedSecret, // strictly, P-256 x coordinate is 32 bytes, fits AES-256) block, _ := aes.NewCipher(sharedSecret) gcm, _ := cipher.NewGCM(block) plaintext, err := gcm.Open(nil, nonce, ciphertext, nil) return plaintext, err }
title: The Golang4U Cryptography Bible: E2EE, ECIES & Blind Indexing

content: Chapter 4: Privacy & The Blind IndexWe treat user data (Email) as toxic waste. We encrypt it at rest. User.EncryptedEmail = a8d29f.... However, we have a problem: Uniqueness. We need to ensure bob@gmail.com doesn’t sign up twice. But Encrypt("bob@gmail.com") produces a different ciphertext every time (because of the random Nonce). We cannot query WHERE email = '...'.
title: The Golang4U Cryptography Bible: E2EE, ECIES & Blind Indexing

content: 4.1 The Solution: HMAC Blind IndexingWe create a separate field: BlindIndex. This is a deterministic hash. $$Index = HMAC_{SHA256}(Email, Server_Secret_Search_Key)$$ We store: EncryptedEmail: Use for sending emails (Decryptable). BlindIndex: Use for searching/uniqueness (Not Decryptable).
title: The Golang4U Cryptography Bible: E2EE, ECIES & Blind Indexing

content: 4.2 Why HMAC? Why not SHA256?Plain SHA256(email) is vulnerable to Rainbow Tables. An attacker can pre-calculate the hash of every email on earth. HMAC requires a Secret Key. If the database leaks, the attacker has the hashes, but not the Secret Key. They cannot reverse the hashes (because hashes are one-way), and they cannot brute-force them (because they don’t have the key). In internal/service/user_service.go: // Calculate Blind Index hash := hmac.New(sha256.New, []byte(os.Getenv("SEARCH_KEY"))) hash.Write([]byte(plainEmail)) index := hex.EncodeToString(hash.Sum(nil)) // Check DB if s.db.Exists("idx_email_" + index) { return Error("Email Taken") } This guarantees k-anonymity and uniqueness simultaneously.
title: The Golang4U Cryptography Bible: E2EE, ECIES & Blind Indexing

content: Chapter 5: Frontend Integration (Web Crypto)The backend is only half the story. The browser must do the encryption. We use the native window.crypto.subtle API. No npm install. ImportKey: Browser imports Server Public Key (SPKI). GenerateKey: Browser makes ephemeral EC Keypair. DeriveKey: ECDH + AES-GCM context. Encrypt: AES-GCM Encrypt password. Export: Pack bytes and Hex encode. This ensures that the plaintext password never travels over the network.
title: The Golang4U Cryptography Bible: E2EE, ECIES & Blind Indexing

content: ConclusionWe have built a system where: Secrecy: Only the Server can read the data (ECIES). Privacy: Even the DB admin cannot read the data (AES-GCM at rest). Integrity: No one can tamper with the data (GCM Tags). Searchability: We can still enforce rules (Blind Indexing). This is cryptographic engineering at its finest.
title: The Golang4U Cryptography Bible: E2EE, ECIES & Blind Indexing

content: The definitive guide to the Golang4U authentication system. We explore the move from JWT to PASETO v4, the implementation of PASERK key management, and the custom Echo middleware verifying every request.
title: The Golang4U Authentication Bible: PASETO, Usage & Design

content: Preface: Authentication vs AuthorizationFirst, a distinction. Authentication (AuthN): “Who are you?” (I am User 123). Authorization (AuthZ): “What can you do?” (I can delete posts). This, guide focuses on AuthN. specifically, how we securely identify a user across stateless HTTP requests.
title: The Golang4U Authentication Bible: PASETO, Usage & Design

content: Chapter 1: The Fall of JWT (JSON Web Tokens)For a decade, JWT (RFC 7519) was the king. But heavy lies the crown. A JWT is a string: header.payload.signature.
title: The Golang4U Authentication Bible: PASETO, Usage & Design

content: The Design Flaw: Cipher AgilityThe header tells the server how to verify the token. { "alg": "HS256", "typ": "JWT" } This “Cipher Agility” is a disaster. Alg=“None” Attack: Attackers change HS256 to None and strip the signature. Many libraries defaulted to trusting the header. Algorithm Confusion: Attackers change RS256 (Asymmetric) to HS256 (Symmetric). They sign the token using the Public Key (which they have) as the “Secret Key”. The server verifies it using the Public Key (thinking it’s the Secret Key). It matches. hacked.
title: The Golang4U Authentication Bible: PASETO, Usage & Design

content: The PASETO SolutionPASETO (Platform-Agnostic Security Tokens) removes the choice. Format: v4.public.payload.footer v4: This Version implies exactly Ed25519 for signatures. No negotiation. public: This Purpose implies Asymmetric crypto. If you send a v2 token, the server rejects it. If you send a local token to a public endpoint, the server rejects it. The protocol is strict.
title: The Golang4U Authentication Bible: PASETO, Usage & Design

content: Chapter 2: The Key Standard (PASERK)Managing keys is hard. Is this 32-byte string an AES key? An Ed25519 Seed? A Curve25519 Point? We use PASERK (Platform-Agnostic SERialized Keys).
title: The Golang4U Authentication Bible: PASETO, Usage & Design

content: 2.1 The Formatk4.local.A8F92... k4: Version 4. local: Symmetric Key type. Data: Base64URL encoded key.
title: The Golang4U Authentication Bible: PASETO, Usage & Design

content: 2.2 Parsing Logic (internal/token/paseto.go)We enforce this format in our code. func getV4SymmetricKey(keyStr string) (paseto.V4SymmetricKey, error) { // 1. Check Prefix (Type Safety) if !strings.HasPrefix(keyStr, "k4.local.") { return paseto.V4SymmetricKey{}, fmt.Errorf("invalid key format") } // 2. Decode Payload encoded := strings.TrimPrefix(keyStr, "k4.local.") bytes, _ := base64.RawURLEncoding.DecodeString(encoded) // 3. Import Key return paseto.V4SymmetricKeyFromBytes(bytes) } This prevents “Key Confusion” at the configuration level. You cannot accidentally use a v2 key.
title: The Golang4U Authentication Bible: PASETO, Usage & Design

content: Chapter 3: The Token Maker (PasetoMaker)In internal/token/paseto.go, we define the Maker interface. type Maker interface { CreateToken(username string, duration time.Duration) (string, *Payload, error) VerifyToken(token string) (*Payload, error) }
title: The Golang4U Authentication Bible: PASETO, Usage & Design

content: 3.1 Creating the TokenWhen CreateUser or Login succeeds, we mint a token: func (maker *PasetoMaker) CreateToken(username string, duration time.Duration) (string, *Payload, error) { tokenObj := paseto.NewToken() // Standard Claims (RFC 7519 mapping) tokenObj.SetJti(uuid.NewString()) // Unique ID tokenObj.SetIssuedAt(time.Now()) // iat tokenObj.SetNotBefore(time.Now()) // nbf tokenObj.SetExpiration(time.Now().Add(duration)) // exp // Custom Claims tokenObj.Set("username", username) tokenObj.Set("role", "user") // Encrypt (Symmetric V4 Local) encrypted := tokenObj.V4Encrypt(maker.symmetricKey, nil) return encrypted, payload, nil } Why specific timestamps? IssuedAt: Good for audit logs. NotBefore: Prevents a token from being used if “created in the future” (Clock Skew protection). Expiration: Mandatory.
title: The Golang4U Authentication Bible: PASETO, Usage & Design

content: 3.2 Verifying the TokenThis is the most critical function in the system. func (maker *PasetoMaker) VerifyToken(token string) (*Payload, error) { parser := paseto.NewParser() // 1. Rule: Must not be expired parser.AddRule(paseto.NotExpired()) // 2. Rule: Must NOT have a footer (Anti-Tamper) // Attackers sometimes hide data in unencrypted footers. // We enforce a "Closed System". // (Note: library specific implementation varies, manual check below) tokenObj, err := parser.ParseV4Local(maker.symmetricKey, token, nil) if err != nil { return nil, ErrInvalidToken } // 3. Manual Footer Check if len(tokenObj.Footer()) > 0 { return nil, fmt.Errorf("footer not allowed") } return payloadFromToken(tokenObj), nil }
title: The Golang4U Authentication Bible: PASETO, Usage & Design

content: Chapter 4: The Middleware (PasetoMW)How do we protect routes? In internal/paseto_middleware/paseto.go.
title: The Golang4U Authentication Bible: PASETO, Usage & Design

content: 4.1 Lookup StrategyWe support multiple clients (Web, CLI, Mobile). We look for the token in this order: Cookie: access_token (Web Browser, prevents XSS reading). Header: Authorization: Bearer ... (CLI/Mobile/Postman). func createTokenExtractor(lookup "cookie:access_token,header:Authorization") { // splits string and returns a function that checks cookie then header }
title: The Golang4U Authentication Bible: PASETO, Usage & Design

content: 4.2 The Interceptor func (pmw *PasetoMW) Paseto(next echo.HandlerFunc) echo.HandlerFunc { return func(c echo.Context) error { // 1. Extract Token tokenStr := extractToken(c) if tokenStr == "" { return c.JSON(401, "Missing Token") } // 2. Verify Crypto payload, err := pmw.maker.VerifyToken(tokenStr) if err != nil { return c.JSON(401, "Invalid Token") } // 3. Inject into Context // This is why handlers can do: user := c.Get("user") c.Set("user", payload) return next(c) } }
title: The Golang4U Authentication Bible: PASETO, Usage & Design

content: Chapter 5: Access vs Refresh StrategyWe use a Dual Token System.
title: The Golang4U Authentication Bible: PASETO, Usage & Design

content: 5.1 Access Token (The “Wristband”) Type: PASETO v4 Local. Lifetime: 15 Minutes. Storage: HttpOnly Cookie. Logic: Stateless. If the signature is valid, you are in.
title: The Golang4U Authentication Bible: PASETO, Usage & Design

content: 5.2 Refresh Token (The “Ticket Stub”) Type: PASETO v4 Local (Different Key!). Lifetime: 7 Days. Storage: HttpOnly Cookie (Path=/refresh). Logic: Stateful. The Refresh Flow: Access Token expires (401). Frontend calls POST /refresh (Browser sends Refresh Cookie automatically). Server verifies Refresh Token signature. Critical Step: Server checks DB: “Is User 123 Banned? Is Version matches?” If OK, Server issues NEW Access Token (15 mins) and NEW Refresh Token (7 days). Why Rotate Refresh Tokens? If a hacker steals your Refresh Token, they have 7 days of access. By Rotating it (issuing a new one on every use), we detect theft. If the Hacker uses the Old Token -> We detect reuse -> We invalid the entire family of tokens. (Reuse Detection).
title: The Golang4U Authentication Bible: PASETO, Usage & Design

content: ConclusionGolang4U’s Auth system is not just “import a library.” It is a carefully designed machine: Strict Crypto: PASETO v4 + PASERK. Strict Middleware: Order of operations (Cookie -> Header -> Verify). Strict Lifecycle: Access (15m) / Refresh (7d) Rotation. This provides the speed of stateless architecture with the security controls of stateful sessions.
title: The Golang4U Authentication Bible: PASETO, Usage & Design

content: A definitive guide to securing a Go backend. We dissect the `ipFilter` middleware (Mutex/Radix Tree), the `Tollbooth` rate limiter (Token Bucket), and the rigorous HSTS/CSP header configuration that protects Golang4U users.
title: The Golang4U Security Bible: A Defense-in-Depth Masterclass

content: Preface: The Zero Trust MindsetSecurity is often treated as a feature. “Add a login page, and we’re secure.” This is false. Security is a Process. It is the sum of every line of code that handles input. In Golang4U, we adopt a Zero Trust mindset. Trust No IP: Even if it didn’t attack us yesterday, it might attack us today. Trust No User: Even if they have a valid token, they might be spamming. Trust No Browser: Even if Chrome says it’s secure, we enforce it with headers. This guide will walk you through the three rings of defense: Network, Application, and Presentation.
title: The Golang4U Security Bible: A Defense-in-Depth Masterclass

content: Chapter 1: The Network Layer (IP Filtering)Before a request can even touch our business logic, it must pass the IP Filter. This is our “Bouncer.”
title: The Golang4U Security Bible: A Defense-in-Depth Masterclass

content: 1.1 The Architecture of internal/ipFilterWe don’t use a simple map[string]bool. Why? Because IP ranges exist. Blocking 192.168.1.0/24 means blocking 256 addresses. A map cannot handle CIDR ranges efficiently. We use a Radix Tree (via github.com/jpillora/ipfilter). Time Complexity: $O(k)$ where $k$ is the number of bits in the IP (32 for IPv4, 128 for IPv6). Space Complexity: Extremely efficient. It compresses common prefixes.
title: The Golang4U Security Bible: A Defense-in-Depth Masterclass

content:
1.2 The Implementation (ip_filter.go)Let’s look at the IPFilter struct in internal/ipFilter/ip_filter.go. type IPFilter struct { ipBlockList *ipfilter.IPFilter // The Radix Tree Engine writer *bufio.Writer // Buffered Writer for Persistence file *os.File // File Handle mu sync.Mutex // The "Bathroom Key" } The Concurrency Problem: Echo is multi-threaded. If two distinct requests try to ban an IP at the same time, they will race to write to bannedIps.txt. Thread A writes: “1.2.3.4
” Thread B writes: “5.6.7.8
” Without a lock, the OS might interleave the bytes: “1.2.35.6.7.4.8
”. The file is now corrupt. The Solution (Mutex): func (f *IPFilter) BlockIP(ip string) error { f.mu.Lock() // STOP. Only one thread passes. defer f.mu.Unlock() // OK, carry on. // 1. Update Memory (Instant) f.ipBlockList.BlockIP(ip) // 2. Update Disk (Persistent) if _, err := f.writer.WriteString(ip + "
"); err != nil { return err } // 3. Flush (Durability) // We force the OS to write the buffer to disk immediately. return f.writer.Flush() }
title: The Golang4U Security Bible: A Defense-in-Depth Masterclass

content: 1.3 The Middleware HookIn server.go, we see: s.e.Use(s.ipfilter.IPBlockerMiddleware) Inside IPBlockerMiddleware: func (f *IPFilter) IPBlockerMiddleware(next echo.HandlerFunc) echo.HandlerFunc { return func(c echo.Context) error { // Critical: c.RealIP() parses X-Forwarded-For headers ip := c.RealIP() if f.ipBlockList.Blocked(ip) { // We return 403 Forbidden immediately. // The request NEVER reaches the Database. return c.String(http.StatusForbidden, "Your IP is banned.") } return next(c) } }
title: The Golang4U Security Bible: A Defense-in-Depth Masterclass

content: Chapter 2: The Application Layer (Rate Limiting)Once the IP is allowed in, we must ensure they behave. A “Good” user might turn “Bad” if their script malfunctions and hits our API 1,000 times a second. We use Tollbooth (a generic middleware for rate limiting).
title: The Golang4U Security Bible: A Defense-in-Depth Masterclass

content: 2.1 The Token Bucket AlgorithmImagine a bucket with a small hole in the bottom. Tokens (Water) drip out at a steady rate (1 request/second). Burst Capacity: The size of the bucket (5 requests). Action: Using the API adds water. Overflow: If the bucket is full, the water spills (Request Rejected). This allows a user to “click fast” for a few seconds (burst), but prevents sustained spam.
title: The Golang4U Security Bible: A Defense-in-Depth Masterclass

content: 2.2 Granular ApplicationWe don’t rate limit everything equally. Serving Images: Fast, Cheap. Limit = 100 req/sec. Hashing Passwords: Slow, Expensive (Argon2). Limit = 1 req/sec. In server.go (EstablishRoutes): // Only limit the Login route aggressively s.e.POST("/login", s.h.Login, s.rateLimit.Middleware)
title: The Golang4U Security Bible: A Defense-in-Depth Masterclass

content: Chapter 3: The Presentation Layer (Secure Headers)The browser is a hostile environment. We use HTTP Headers to configure the browser’s security sandbox. Configured in internal/server/server.go via middleware.SecureWithConfig.
title: The Golang4U Security Bible: A Defense-in-Depth Masterclass

content: 3.1 HSTS (Strict-Transport-Security)The Vulnerability: SSL Stripping. A hacker sits in a coffee shop Wi-Fi. You type golang4u.com. Your browser sends GET http://golang4u.com. The hacker intercepts this unencrypted packet and proxies the connection. You never see the padlock. The Fix: HSTSMaxAge: 31536000, // 1 Year This header tells Chrome: “For the next 365 days, NEVER send an unencrypted packet to this domain. Internalize the redirect to HTTPS.”
title: The Golang4U Security Bible: A Defense-in-Depth Masterclass

content: 3.2 X-Frame-OptionsThe Vulnerability: Clickjacking. A site win-iphone.com loads golang4u.com/delete-account in an invisible <iframe>. The user clicks “Claim Prize” on the parent page, but the click passes through to the “Delete” button on your site. The Fix: XFrameOptions: "SAMEORIGIN", This tells the browser: “Only page on golang4u.com can iframe golang4u.com.”
title: The Golang4U Security Bible: A Defense-in-Depth Masterclass

content: 3.3 CSP (Content-Security-Policy)The Vulnerability: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting). A user posts a comment: <script>stealCookies()</script>. If you render this, the script runs in everyone’s browser. The Fix: ContentSecurityPolicy: "default-src 'self'", This tells the browser: “Only load scripts from My Domain. If you see a script pointing to evil.com, BLOCK IT.”
title: The Golang4U Security Bible: A Defense-in-Depth Masterclass

content: Chapter 4: Data Layer Defense (The Blind Index)We touched on this in Architecture, but let’s look at the Security implications. Problem: We encrypt emails in the DB (EncryptedEmail). But we need to stop duplicate signups. Naive Solution: Decrypt every row to check. (Slow + Insecure). Insecure Solution: Store Hash(email). (Rainbow Table Attack possible). The Secure Solution: HMAC-SHA256 Blind Index. // internal/service/user_service.go key := "idx_email_" + Hex(HMAC(email, SecretKey)) HMAC: Hash-based Message Authentication Code. It is impossible to reverse the hash without the SecretKey (stored in ENV, not DB). If the DB leaks, the attacker sees idx_email_a8f92.... They cannot guess the email because they don’t have the Secret Key to generate the hashes for their dictionary attack. This is k-anonymity.
title: The Golang4U Security Bible: A Defense-in-Depth Masterclass

content: Chapter 5: Docker & Infrastructure SecuritySecurity doesn’t stop at Go code.
title: The Golang4U Security Bible: A Defense-in-Depth Masterclass

content: 5.1 The Rootless ContainerIn our Dockerfile, we should never run as root. # Create a group and user RUN addgroup -S appgroup && adduser -S appuser -G appgroup USER appuser If a hacker exploits a vulnerability in Echo to get Remote Code Execution (RCE), they are trapped as appuser. They cannot install packages, modify system files, or read /etc/shadow.
title: The Golang4U Security Bible: A Defense-in-Depth Masterclass

content: 5.2 Secrets ManagementWe NEVER commit secrets to Git. We use config/config.go to read from Environment Variables. config.GmailToken = os.Getenv("GMAIL_TOKEN") In production (Kubernetes), these are injected as k8s Secrets.
title: The Golang4U Security Bible: A Defense-in-Depth Masterclass

content: ConclusionReview the checklist for Golang4U: IP Filter: Stops the bots at the door. Rate Limit: Stops the flooding. HSTS/CSP: Stops the browser tricks. HMAC Index: Stops the DB leak from revealing emails. Rootless Docker: Stops the RCE from taking over the server. This is what “Production Ready” looks like.
title: The Golang4U Security Bible: A Defense-in-Depth Masterclass

content: The definitive, deep-dive guide to the Golang4U backend architecture. We deconstruct the codebase from the entry point in `cmd` to the database layer in `internal`, explaining every design decision, dependency injection pattern, and folder structure choice along the way. This is a complete engineering handbook.
title: The Golang4U Architecture: A Service-Oriented Masterclass

content: Preface: Why Read This?If you are just starting with Go, you might write everything in main.go. It works for a “Hello World,” but it fails for a production system. If you are an expert, you might argue about “Clean Architecture” vs “Hexagonal” vs “Onion.” Golang4U adopts a pragmatic, production-ready Service-Oriented Architecture (SOA) structure. It is designed to be: Testable: Every layer can be mocked. Scalable: New features (like a “Video” post type) don’t break old ones. Readable: A new developer knows exactly where to put code. This guide is not a summary. It is a Masterclass. We will read the code together, line by line, layer by layer. By the end, you will understand not just how it works, but why it was built this way.
title: The Golang4U Architecture: A Service-Oriented Masterclass

content: Chapter 1: The Blueprint (Folder Structure)Go is infamous for not having a standard structure. However, the community has coalesced around the Standard Go Project Layout. We define our project by What it is, not What it does.
title: The Golang4U Architecture: A Service-Oriented Masterclass

content: 1.1 The High-Level Mapgraph TD Root[golang4u_server] Root --> Cmd[cmd/] Root --> Internal[internal/] Root --> Pkg[pkg/] Cmd --> ServerMain[server/main.go] Internal --> Handler[handler/] Internal --> Service[service/] Internal --> Repository[repository/] Internal --> Model[model/] Internal --> Config[config/] Internal --> Security[security/]
title: The Golang4U Architecture: A Service-Oriented Masterclass

content: 1.2 cmd/: The Entry PointThis folder is the “Main Entrance.” It contains the main package. Rule: Minimal logic. This file should just parse flags, read config, and call server.Run(). Why?: By keeping main small, we allow others to import our application code (in internal) without running the server.
title: The Golang4U Architecture: A Service-Oriented Masterclass

content: 1.3 internal/: The Private CoreIn Go 1.4+, directories named internal are special. The Go compiler forbids external projects from importing packages inside internal. Why?: This enforces API boundaries. We are free to break things inside internal without worrying about breaking 3rd-party users of our library. The Layers: Handler: Speaking HTTP (Parsing JSON, Status Codes). Service: Business Logic (Validation, Encryption, Emailing). Repository: Data Access (SQL, Mongo, Redis).
title: The Golang4U Architecture: A Service-Oriented Masterclass

content: 1.4 pkg/: The Public LibraryCode here is safe for anyone to use. Example: pkg/utils might contain a helper to format dates. Rule: No business logic here. Just generic tools.
title: The Golang4U Architecture: A Service-Oriented Masterclass

content: Chapter 2: Dependency Injection (The Wiring)The most critical pattern in Golang4U is Dependency Injection (DI). Many beginners use Global Variables for database connections (var DB *sql.DB). This is the root of all evil. It makes parallel testing impossible (tests overwrite each other’s DB). It hides dependencies (you don’t know function X uses the DB).
title: The Golang4U Architecture: A Service-Oriented Masterclass

content: 2.1 The Constructor PatternWe use “Constructor Functions” (factories) to create our structs. In internal/handler/handler.go: type Handler struct { DB database.DBStore // Interface! data *ttlcache.Cache[string, any] PostService *service.PostService UserService *service.UserService } // The "Constructor" func NewHandler(db database.DBStore, ps *service.PostService, ...) *Handler { return &Handler{ DB: db, PostService: ps, // ... } } Key Takeaway: The Handler asks for what it needs. It doesn’t build it.
title: The Golang4U Architecture: A Service-Oriented Masterclass

content: 2.2 The Composition Root (server.go)If everyone asks for dependencies, who creates them? The Composition Root. In our case, SetupServer in internal/server/server.go. func SetupServer(db database.DBStore, config *config.Config) *Server { // 1. Create Services (injecting DB) userService := service.NewUserService(db, ...) postService := service.NewPostService(db, ...) // 2. Create Handlers (injecting Services) h := handler.NewHandler(config, db, userSvc, postSvc, ...) // 3. Create Router (injecting Handlers) e := echo.New() // ... wiring routes ... return &Server{e: e, h: h} } This creates a clear dependency graph: Router -> Handler -> Service -> Repo -> DB. It is an Acyclic Graph. (No circles).
title: The Golang4U Architecture: A Service-Oriented Masterclass

content: Chapter 3: The Presentation Layer (Handler)The Handler layer is the Diplomat. It speaks the language of the Web (HTTP). Its job is to translate JSON into Go Structs, call the Service, and translate results back to JSON. It must NEVER contain business logic.
title: The Golang4U Architecture: A Service-Oriented Masterclass

content: Detailed Walkthrough: HandleFormSubmissionLet’s look at a complex handler in internal/handler/handler.go. func (h *Handler) HandleFormSubmission(c echo.Context) error { // 1. Protocol Decoding formType := c.Param("formType") // "news", "jobs", etc. // 2. Security Check (Virus Scan) // The handler knows about 'filescan', but not 'how' to scan. if err := h.fs.ScanData(c, nil); err != nil { return err // 403 Forbidden or 500 Internal Error } // 3. User Context (Authentication) // We retrieve the authenticated user from the request context/token. userStore, err := GetAvatar(c, h.TTLDB, h.DB) if err != nil { return err } // 4. State Validation (Handler Logic) // "Is the user banned? Is the user verified?" // This is borderline business logic, but it's acceptable here // as it gates access to the service call. if userStore.Disable { return c.JSON(http.StatusForbidden, "Disabled") } // 5. Routing Logic switch formType { case "news": return h.handleNews(c, ctx) case "learn": return h.handleLearn(c, ctx) // ... } }
title: The Golang4U Architecture: A Service-Oriented Masterclass

content: The Sub-Handlers patternNotice handleNews. The main handler is getting too big, so we split it. func (h *Handler) handleNews(c echo.Context, ctx context.Context) error { // A. Bind (JSON -> Struct) data := new(formdata.NewsFormData) if err := c.Bind(data); err != nil { return err } // B. Validate (Struct Tags) if err := c.Validate(data); err != nil { return err } // C. File Handling // The handler knows about Multipart Forms. The Service does not. // So the handler extracts the []byte here. data.NewsCover, _ = readFile(c, "news-cover") // D. Call Service return h.PostService.CreateNews(ctx, data) } Why extract the file bytes here? If we passed c *echo.Context to the Service, the Service would depend on echo (HTTP). That violates our layering. By extracting []byte, the Service receives pure data. It can be tested without a web server.
title: The Golang4U Architecture: A Service-Oriented Masterclass

content: Chapter 4: The Business Layer (Service)The Service layer is the Brain. It contains the rules of the application. “Users must be 18+.” “Passwords must be encrypted.” “Emails must be unique.”
title: The Golang4U Architecture: A Service-Oriented Masterclass

content: Case Study: UserService.CreateUserIn internal/service/user_service.go: func (s *UserService) CreateUser(newUser *user.User) error { // Logic 1: Decryption (Privacy) // The raw request has encrypted fields. We unlock them here. plainEmail, _ := security.DecryptECIES(s.privKey, newUser.EncrypedEmail) // Logic 2: Blind Indexing (Uniqueness) // Check if email exists without storing plain email. hash := sha256.Sum256(plainEmail) if s.repo.Exists(hash) { return Error("Already Registered") } // Logic 3: Roles if s.repo.Count() == 0 { newUser.Role = "admin" // First user is King } // Logic 4: Persistence return s.repo.Save(newUser) } Notice what is missing: No c.JSON. The service returns error or struct. It doesn’t know about JSON. No http.StatusForbidden. It returns domain errors (ErrDuplicateUser).
title: The Golang4U Architecture: A Service-Oriented Masterclass

content: Chapter 5: The Data Layer (Repository)The Repository layer is the Librarian. It knows how to talk to the database. We define it using an Interface in internal/database/database.go. type DBStore interface { GetUserStore(key string) (interface{}, error) SetUserStore(key string, value interface{}) error CountUsers() (int64, error) // ... }
title: The Golang4U Architecture: A Service-Oriented Masterclass

content: Why usage Interface? (The Mocking Power)Imagine writing a test for Service.CreateUser. If Service depended on *mongo.Client, you would need to run a MongoDB Docker container just to run go test. That’s slow. With an interface, we can do this: // mocks/db_mock.go type MockDB struct { users map[string]interface{} } func (m *MockDB) SetUserStore(key string, val interface{}) error { m.users[key] = val return nil } Now our unit tests run in milliseconds.
title: The Golang4U Architecture: A Service-Oriented Masterclass

content: The “Store” Wrapper PatternGolang4U uses a NoSQL database (MongoDB implied by key-value semantics in database.go). But we don’t just dump the User struct. We wrap it. type Store struct { User User // The Public Profile ReferalCodes []ReferalCode // Internal Referral Data Disable bool // Admin Flag Lifetime time.Time // TTL for temp users } This “Metadata Wrapper” allows us to add system-level flags (like Disable) without polluting the User object that might be returned to the frontend Main API.
title: The Golang4U Architecture: A Service-Oriented Masterclass

content: Chapter 6: Cross-Cutting ConcernsSome logic touches every layer.
title: The Golang4U Architecture: A Service-Oriented Masterclass

content: 6.1 Configuration (config/)We load config once in main, and pass it down. Handler needs config.ClamavURL. Service needs config.GmailToken. This is passed via the Constructor, ensuring every component has explicitly declared its configuration needs.
title: The Golang4U Architecture: A Service-Oriented Masterclass

content: 6.2 Security (security/ & ipfilter/)Security is often implemented as Middleware (wrapping the Handler). IPFilter: Checks IP before Handler logic. RateLimit: Checking frequency. PASETO: Checks Auth Tokens. But deep security (Encryption) happens in Service (as seen in CreateUser).
title: The Golang4U Architecture: A Service-Oriented Masterclass

content: Chapter 7: Error Handling StrategyGo errors are values. In golang4u, we propagate them up. Repository: Returns mongo.ErrNoDocuments. Service: Wraps it: fmt.Errorf("user not found: %w", err). Handler: Unwraps it (using errors.Is) and decides the HTTP status. If user not found -> 404 Not Found. If db connection failed -> 500 Internal Error. This keeps the “HTTPness” in the handler. The Service shouldn’t decide if an error is a 400 or a 404; it just says “It failed because X”.
title: The Golang4U Architecture: A Service-Oriented Masterclass

content: ConclusionThe Golang4U architecture is an exercise in Discipline. It is tempting to just write a SQL query inside a Handler. It is tempting to just use a global var DB. But by adhering to this Service-Oriented-Architecture, we gain: Isolation: Bugs in the DB layer don’t break the HTTP layer logic. Clarity: New developers know exactly where to put new code. Confidence: We can test every piece in isolation. This is the standard for professional Go engineering.
title: The Golang4U Architecture: A Service-Oriented Masterclass
